RescueVision is a proposed disaster-response support platform for police, ambulance teams, hospital coordinators, and other authorized emergency-service users. It combines the presentation of available damage-assessment information with two-dimensional and three-dimensional area views, person-related assistance records, reported hazards, and response guidance. Through a website and mobile application, the project aims to help users understand an affected area, coordinate assistance, and maintain response-status information while retaining human responsibility for decisions.

Understanding disaster impacts and preparing for effective response are central concerns in disaster risk reduction. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 identifies understanding disaster risk and strengthening preparedness for effective response among its priorities [1]. This context motivates the investigation of systems that help emergency organizations interpret and share relevant information.

Remote sensing offers one source of information about the physical effects of a disaster. Gupta et al. introduce xBD, a dataset containing pre-disaster and post-disaster satellite imagery, building annotations, and damage labels for research into change detection and building damage assessment [2]. This supports the investigation of image-based assessment as an input to situational awareness. It does not establish the accuracy or effectiveness of RescueVision, which requires its own evaluation.

The proposed RescueVision scenario also involves information that imagery alone cannot establish: people awaiting assistance, reported hazards, changing street conditions, and the status of a response. The motivation is to place these information types in a coherent spatial and case-based context. A user should be able to understand what a record represents, where it applies, and whether its information is current or requires confirmation.

Responsible handling of this information is part of the project motivation. OCHA describes data responsibility as the safe, ethical, and effective management of personal and non-personal data in humanitarian action, and notes that disclosure of sensitive data may cause harm [3]. RescueVision therefore treats access to person-related information and the interpretation of uncertain observations as design concerns from the beginning.

The purpose of this Software Requirements Specification (SRS) introduction is to define the problem, intended audience, intended use, scope, terminology, and constraints of RescueVision. It establishes a common foundation for the system description, detailed requirements, and design presented in the subsequent report sections.

The document supports communication among the project team, supervisor, assessors, and relevant stakeholders. Its objectives and boundaries provide a basis for deciding which capabilities belong to the proposal and for checking that later requirements and design decisions describe the same system. The success criteria identify observable outcomes to be used when planning verification.

This chapter describes intended behavior and proposed evaluation targets. Implementation status and experimental findings belong in the prototype and evaluation sections and must be supported by the evidence presented there.

RescueVision is intended to support the review of a disaster-affected area by authorized emergency-service users. The website is envisaged as an environment for overview and coordination, while the mobile application supports relevant field interactions. Detailed user privileges are specified in the system-description and requirements sections.

A typical proposed use begins when incident-related information becomes available. This may include imagery used for damage assessment and separately supplied records concerning people, hazards, or response activities. An authorized user examines the area, selects a relevant record, reviews the information and its limitations, and records or coordinates the next action. Subsequent updates maintain the status of the assistance case.

Two-dimensional and three-dimensional views provide alternative spatial presentations where suitable data exist. Person tracking means following available person-related location or status updates within an authorized workflow. It does not establish continuous observation or automatic identification of people. Responder location and the location of a person requiring assistance are separate record types and must not be confused.

Route guidance is intended to help users interpret available movement options using relevant road and hazard information. The user remains responsible for assessing its suitability. A route is not a guarantee of current accessibility or safety. Similarly, image-derived damage information does not establish building occupancy, injury, or structural safety.

For the academic project, these activities are to be demonstrated through controlled scenarios and genuine preliminary evidence appropriate to the implementation stage. A demonstration does not establish readiness for operational emergency deployment.

RescueVision addresses the problem of presenting different types of disaster-related information in a form that supports a shared understanding of the affected area. In the proposed scenario, damage observations, assistance needs, hazard reports, and response updates may originate from different sources and may refer to different times. Users must determine how these records relate geographically and which information is suitable for a decision.

Fragmented information can create specific difficulties in this scenario. A recorded assistance need may lack a verified location; an otherwise relevant street may have a newly reported obstruction; and a responder may not know whether another organization is already handling a case. The project investigates how spatial presentation and structured case updates can make these relationships visible. These are the problems defining the proposed use scenario, rather than claims that every emergency organization follows the same procedures.

The central project question is how to combine available assessment information and response records while preserving their source, update status, and uncertainty. The intended contribution is a coherent workflow for review and coordination. Demonstrating reduced response time or improved rescue outcomes would require a separate operational evaluation.

The proposed platform connects an assessment component with a response-support environment. Suitable before-and-after imagery can provide a basis for building-related damage predictions and visual summaries. These analytical outputs are presented alongside separately sourced person-related records, reported hazards, and response information. Their common spatial context helps the user examine relationships without treating one information type as proof of another.

The website and mobile application are intended to support the progression from viewing an incident area to reviewing a case, coordinating an action, and updating its status. Detailed technology choices and model architectures are addressed in later sections; this chapter defines their intended role and boundaries.

The project aim is to support situational awareness and assistance coordination through an understandable presentation of available disaster-related information. Table 1-2 expresses the objectives to which detailed requirements and verification activities should be linked.
Provide a consistent spatial view of an incident area and its associated records in 2D and 3D where suitable data exist.
Present image-derived damage information with a clear link to its input case and interpretation limits.
Support review of people who may require assistance and reported hazards, including location and information status.
Support coordination through defined user responsibilities and traceable response-status updates.
Support informed route selection using available road and hazard information, including cases where guidance cannot be produced.
Make missing, outdated, or uncertain information visible and restrict actions according to defined user permissions.

Table 1-3 defines the proposed scope. Each included capability must have a corresponding requirement and design explanation. The table describes the intended platform rather than asserting that every capability has been implemented.
Present the affected area and associated records in 2D and 3D. Suitable spatial data are required; complete or live reconstruction is not assumed.
Present image-derived building and damage information. Outputs do not certify structural safety or establish the presence of people.
Organize available information about people who may need help and the status of the response. Automatic discovery of every affected person is outside the claimed scope.
Present available location or status updates in the permitted workflow. Continuous, precise, real-time tracking is not guaranteed.
Display recorded hazards and relevant details. An absence of markers does not establish an absence of hazards.
Support case review and status updates by defined roles. Command authority remains with the responsible organizations.
Present guidance using available network and hazard data. Guaranteed fastest or safest routes and unrestricted vehicle access are outside the claimed scope.
Summarize available assessment information. Reports retain the limitations of the source data and predictions.
Describe relevant information exchanges and dependencies. Live integration with government, hospital, or dispatch systems is not assumed.

The proposal does not include autonomous dispatch, medical diagnosis, certified structural inspection, or guaranteed rescue outcomes. Detecting people beneath debris from ordinary RGB imagery is not a claimed capability. Geographic coverage and demonstration datasets are bounded by the data selected for evaluation.

Table 1-4 defines proposed acceptance scenarios for the intended platform. They are observable targets for review and future testing, not achieved results. For each scenario, the evaluation record should identify the input fixture, user role, expected outcome, actual outcome, and pass or fail result. Capabilities demonstrated only through designs must be reported as design evidence rather than passing software tests.
Using a prepared incident scene, select the same record in 2D and 3D. Pass when both views retain the same record identifier and stored coordinates without changing its case association.

Submit a supported image pair with the required model resources available. Pass when the case returns a damage output and summary linked to that input pair. Test an invalid input separately; pass when failure is explicit and no successful assessment is claimed.
Open prepared person and hazard records. Pass when location, source, update time, and review status are displayed, or each missing field is explicitly identified as unavailable.
Make a permitted response-status update and reopen the case through another authorized session. Pass when the saved status and update attribution are consistent in both sessions.

Use a controlled road network with explicitly blocked edges. Pass when the returned route uses no blocked edge. For a disconnected origin and destination, pass when the system reports that no valid route is available.
Use records designated outdated by the agreed freshness policy and records with missing updates. Pass when neither is presented as current, confirmed information.
Attempt an update using a role without the required permission. Pass when the update is denied and the stored record remains unchanged.

Functional acceptance does not by itself establish model quality. Damage assessment must also be evaluated on a specified held-out dataset, with the split, labels, metrics, and results reported. Suitable measures may include intersection over union for segmentation and per-class precision, recall, and F1 for damage classification. Numerical acceptance thresholds and latency targets must be set before final acceptance testing, using the agreed dataset, hardware, and intended use. No accuracy or speed result is claimed in this chapter.

The proposed features address complementary information needs. Map views provide geographical context, damage layers present analytical observations, and hazard markers identify reported conditions that may affect access. Person-related records connect a possible assistance need with available location and review information.

Coordination features associate these records with permitted user actions and response-status updates. Route guidance supports movement decisions when suitable network information exists. Reports provide a readable summary of an assessment. Each feature must preserve the distinction between observed, predicted, and reviewed information.

Table 1-6 identifies project-specific risks and proposed responses. These mitigations guide later requirements and design; their presence in the proposal does not establish that they have been implemented or tested.
Display update time and availability status; retain a review step before action.
Label predictions, retain access to supporting imagery, and evaluate errors on held-out data.
Define input-quality checks and record conditions that limit interpretation.
Keep person-related evidence separate from image-derived damage assessment.
Use record identifiers and define update responsibility and conflict review.
Show routing assumptions and provide an explicit no-route or unavailable-guidance state.
Minimize personal detail and define access according to role and purpose.
Distinguish pending updates from acknowledged records; show the last successful update time.
Use legends and labels that communicate source, uncertainty, and data age.
Review the shared glossary, objectives, requirements, and diagrams together.

Table 1-8 Constraints and their design implications
Relevance and effect on the proposal
GPU access, imagery, hosting, storage, and external services may incur costs. Scope must fit the resources available to the team, with essential functions distinguished from optional extensions.
Cloud, smoke, poor visibility, and changing local conditions may limit observations. The design must communicate input limitations and avoid treating missing evidence as evidence of safety.
Imagery, personal information, and software may have restrictions on use and sharing. Record provenance, review resource permissions, and define responsible uses before operational deployment.

Users and affected people may differ in digital access, ability, and experience. The proposal must not depend on every person having a smartphone; interfaces should communicate status and warnings clearly.
Imagery and labels from one region may not represent other locations or disaster types. State dataset and geographic boundaries and evaluate generalization before extending claims.
Language, place names, organizational authority, and sharing practices vary. Define the intended context and role responsibilities instead of assuming a universal command structure.
Incorrect predictions or misunderstood routing information may affect decisions. Preserve human review and explicitly communicate unverified or unavailable conditions.
Records concern people who may be vulnerable. Protect dignity, limit unnecessary detail, and avoid equating property damage alone with individual assistance priority.
Person locations and operational details may be sensitive. Specify permitted access, accountable changes, and proportionate data retention; sharing must follow a defined purpose.
Repeated training, processing, and storage consume resources. Consider reuse of suitable outputs, proportionate computation, manageable retention, and maintainable components.

Project I is bounded by the available time, computing resources, data, and preliminary evidence. Suitable imagery, spatial information, and compatible model resources are prerequisites for demonstrating image assessment. Reliable route guidance also depends on a usable network representation and relevant condition data. Person-related functions require a defined information source and update process.

The report must distinguish complete proposed behavior from the subset demonstrated by available evidence. Numerical claims require a stated evaluation method and conditions. Production capacity, continuous availability, and integration with external emergency systems cannot be inferred from a design illustration or a preliminary demonstration.

The design should explain how its decisions address these constraints. Examples include role-based access to sensitive records, indicators of data age, explicit unavailable-information states, and separate representations for predictions and reviewed observations. Important design decisions should be linked to the relevant objective, requirement, or constraint so that their rationale can be assessed.

The literature review examines relevant research and comparable systems. The system description explains the proposed workflow, users, and dependencies. User and system requirements define expected behavior and quality attributes, while the design chapter presents the architecture, information relationships, interactions, and interface concepts. The prototype section presents authentic preliminary evidence and its limits. The discussion and conclusion relate the reported work to its objectives and identify future work.
